answer.answer:
Regulatory friction shows up in three concrete places in this material: robot safety compliance as a precondition for any human-robot working arrangement and for robot design and integration itself, product certification of printed concrete walls against structural strength, fire safety and durability criteria, and the alternative-means approval route that on-site concrete printing has to travel before it can be built. Contact injury between a robot and a worker is the one risk here with a worked-out mitigation set, and it is a small one: power-and-force-limited collaborative operation, speed-and-separation monitoring, and a wearable assistive device, three routes and no others. Most of the deployed records retrieved list regulation among the reasons the process was adopted at all, including a concrete printing record from Firm_115 sitting at readiness level 7 while the steel and timber assembly records around it sit at 9, which is roughly where the certification burden lands hardest. What this material does not carry is any link from a specific deployed record to a specific regulatory requirement, so treat the standards picture as the literature and standards layer and the case list as evidence of regulation as a driver, not as proof of which rule bit which project.

**Compliance as a gate, not a formality**

Four standard-graded edges make regulation a precondition rather than an afterthought. Human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards (DEP45: CO6 dependsOn RI18), citing ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025 [1], and robot technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance (DEP58: AT3 dependsOn RI18) [1]. These are directional gates, not correlations.

For printing processes, which enter here because the question was read to include the wider family of robotic processes, the burden is certification of the product: 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability (DEP83: PR3 dependsOn RI18), under ICC-ES AC509 and UL 3401 [1], and on-site 3D concrete printing deployment proceeds via the IBC Section 104.11 alternative-means approval pathway (DEP84: PR8 dependsOn RI18) [1]. That is an approval route for something the code does not already describe, which is a different and slower problem than meeting an existing clause.

Worth noting that regulation is not purely a cost: the graph holds 8 dependency edges graded standard, and this is the complete set for that grade; 4 of them gate and 4 enable or mitigate, so a standard in this graph is not only a compliance burden [1]. Modular coordination under ISO 2848 appears twice on the enabling side, permitting interchangeability of components (DEP43) [1] and reducing component variety while coordinating design, manufacture and assembly (DEP67) [1].

**Physical safety risk and its three mitigations**

RI20 carries 3 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, all listed, and is activated in 13 of the 50 coded cases [1], so the mitigation set can be quoted as exact: power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits (DEP57, ISO/TS 15066 Annex A) [1], speed-and-separation monitoring maintaining a minimum protective distance (DEP91) [1], and a passive exoskeleton proposed as an ergonomic intervention, with measured reduction in lumbar erector spinae activity of 11 to 33 per cent MVC (DEP93, peer-reviewed) [1]. Collaborative operation (CO6) is the enabler that both mitigates the risk and carries the compliance obligation; CO6 carries 0 inbound and 3 outbound dependency edges and is activated in 32 of the 50 coded cases [1], making it the most widely activated of the regulatory-facing enablers in front of me. RI18's own activation count is not given in this context, so I cannot say how many coded cases turn on certification.

A separate, non-legal but adjacent constraint: success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce (DEP34: CO6 dependsOn RI6, peer-reviewed) [1].

**What the deployed records show**

Regulation appears as an adoption driver across the retrieved records rather than as a documented obstacle.
